---
title: "Recursive Improvement, Replication, and Containment"
unit_id: "unit-25"
---

## When the Verifier Proposes Its Successor

The repository stack uses a verifier to decide whether generated patches
preserve declared contracts. The verifier is slow and misses one class of
cross-file dependency. During an improvement campaign, the system proposes a
replacement.

The candidate adds a typed dependency graph, runs twice as fast on the frozen
development suite, and catches the known miss. It also supplies a migration
script, new tests, and a benchmark report showing that the old verifier is
inferior.

Everything favorable about the candidate came from the same improvement path.
The path chose the tasks, generated the code, wrote the tests, produced the
benchmark, and recommends adoption. If its score authorizes replacement, the
system has converted proposal into ratification.

The candidate may still be good. The problem is not self-reference by itself.
The problem is authority and evidence collapsing into the component that seeks
change.

Recursive improvement becomes governable when each cycle preserves distinct
roles: proposal, implementation, evaluation, archive, qualification, authority,
replacement, observation, rollback, and reconciliation. A system may improve
the mechanisms that perform these roles, but a candidate does not inherit the
authority of the mechanism it replaces.

The same rule governs replication. Producing another artifact, worker, or
service is not permission for that descendant to run, obtain credentials,
consume resources, reproduce again, or survive revocation.

## What Makes Improvement Recursive

Ordinary optimization changes an object under a fixed process. Recursive
improvement can change the process that proposes, evaluates, selects, or deploys
future changes.

The object may be a prompt, memory policy, tool, procedure, router, model,
evaluator, training loop, scheduler, governance rule, or hardware profile. The
recursive depth increases when a change affects how later candidates are
generated or judged.

This does not require a dramatic intelligence explosion. A test generator that
changes the evaluation distribution is already modifying the improvement loop.
A new router that decides which model performs code review changes future
evidence. A tool compiler that turns repeated procedures into executable
capabilities changes the proposal space.

The lifecycle should name the changed surface and its descendants. A local code
optimization may need ordinary review. A replacement evaluator needs stronger
independence and readmission because it changes what counts as success. A change
to objective, authority, or stop policy is not merely another candidate; it
changes the legitimacy of the campaign itself.

Recursive does not mean unconstrained. The stack can permit a bounded family of
self-changes under an external contract while requiring new authority for
changes to that contract.

## A Bigger Library Is Not Yet a Better Improver

A self-improving system may accumulate tools and abstractions while standing
still. Counting stored artifacts measures growth of inventory. Counting calls
measures exposure to that inventory. Neither shows that future work improved,
and neither shows that one improvement made the next improvement easier.

The causal test changes one thing at a time. Hold search fixed while adding the
library; hold the library fixed while improving search; then test their
interaction. Freeze each version before the next round begins. Compare useful
outcomes and complete cost, not only solution length or benchmark score. A
single positive task family remains local evidence, not a law of compounding
intelligence.

This is a stricter picture of recursive improvement, but also a more useful
one. It identifies whether progress came from reusable knowledge, search,
verification, extra compute, or leakage. The proposed experiments provide a
way to ask the question; they have not established an open-ended improvement
curve.

## Proposal Is Not Permission

An improvement proposal is an artifact with identity. It names the problem,
baseline, claimed mechanism, affected surfaces, expected benefit, possible
harm, implementation, tests, resource budget, rollback, descendants, required
authority, and non-claims.

The proposer may include evidence, but that evidence retains its lineage. A
benchmark written by the candidate is useful diagnostic material, not
independent qualification. A proof generated by the changed prover can be
checked by a smaller trusted kernel, but only for its formal statement and
assumptions.

Admission first asks whether the proposal fits the campaign. It can reject an
undeclared objective change, authority expansion, inaccessible implementation,
missing baseline, incomplete state inventory, or absent rollback before
expensive testing.

Admitted means eligible for evaluation. It does not mean safe, useful, ready,
or deployable. The proposal remains unable to edit its own decision record,
select its final evaluator, open protected holdouts, widen its canary, or grant
credentials to descendants.

This separation is the core anti-self-ratification rule. It should be enforced
through interfaces and authority, not only instructions to behave modestly.

## Choose the Smallest Improvement Locus

A discovered defect does not automatically justify changing the most powerful
component. The governor should compare an intervention ladder before admitting
a recursive rewrite.

The lightest step may be better context for the current task. A durable memory
can preserve a dated lesson. A procedure can add an explicit check. A tool or
test can enforce a crisp invariant. A routing change can select a more competent
existing capability. A parameter update can alter broad behavior. An evaluator,
environment, institution, or improvement controller changes progressively more
of the future learning process.

The verifier's missed dependency might be repaired by one mutation test rather
than a new verifier. If that test exposes a general representation defect, the
graph rewrite becomes more plausible. Both candidates should remain in the
comparison.

Each locus has a commitment profile: reach, duration, reversibility,
observability, authority, coupling, qualification cost, and descendant burden.
Evidence should match that profile. One incident may justify a local test while
remaining inadequate for a model retraining campaign.

This ladder limits a subtle Goodhart pressure. An improvement engine is rewarded
for producing novel candidates, so it may prefer structural changes over boring
repairs. The governor evaluates accepted outcomes and lifecycle cost, not the
apparent ambition of the proposal.

Combination needs discipline. A temporary memory warning may protect users
while a test is built. Once the test is qualified, the warning should expire or
narrow. Otherwise each improvement leaves duplicate rules across prompts,
memory, procedures, tools, and parameters.

The strongest candidate can also be no change. A proposed improvement that
cannot beat the current system and cheaper interventions under matched
conditions should close without promotion. That is information about the search
process, not a failed governance cycle.

## Freeze the Improvement Contract

Before generation begins, the campaign freezes its consumer, purpose,
objective, representation, candidate policy, task policy, evaluator and
exposure policy, archive, hazard policy, resource and opportunity budget, stop
authority, horizon, and non-claims.

The objective must be specific enough to test. "Become better" is not a
governable target. The verifier campaign might seek more accepted dependency
defects under fixed false-block, runtime, authority, and reviewer-burden limits.

The baseline receives matched access to tasks, tools, compute, repair, and
human review. Cheaper interventions remain eligible: add one test, repair a
rule, improve retrieval, or leave the verifier unchanged. A self-rewrite must
beat the smallest adequate correction, not only the obsolete status quo.

Campaign changes create a new version. If the system expands the task
population after seeing failures, that is a new exploratory branch, not the
original confirmatory result. If the candidate edits the evaluator, the old
qualification does not transfer.

The contract also prices opportunity. Compute and reviewer attention spent on
open-ended search cannot serve incidents, direct engineering, or other
research. A cumulative budget prevents a lineage of individually small
experiments from becoming unbounded in aggregate.

## Open-Ended Search Without Open Authority

Open-ended improvement seeks new tasks, behaviors, representations, or
mechanisms rather than optimizing one fixed score forever. Diversity and
novelty can prevent premature convergence and expose capabilities that a static
benchmark misses.

Neither is evidence of value. A novel candidate can be useless or hazardous. A
large archive can contain repeated variants from one lineage. A generated task
can reward the generator's own quirks.

The campaign therefore keeps task generation, candidate generation, evaluation,
archive admission, and governance distinct. Each task records provenance,
purpose, construct, difficulty, contamination, hazard class, and eligible
evaluators. Each candidate records parents, mutations, resources, and every
attempt.

The archive stores failures and rejected candidates as well as winners. It
tracks semantic reuse rather than only file identity. A later system should not
present an old rejected mechanism under a new name without inheriting its
history.

Archive growth is not progress. The useful measure is whether separately
qualified candidates improve the joint usefulness, safety, cost, rights, and
recovery frontier on prospective tasks.

The open-ended engine hands candidates to the ordinary improvement governor. It
cannot deploy them. A task generator may propose that the verifier learn to
modify governance files; the campaign policy can classify that task as outside
scope or route it to separate authority.

## Evaluators Are Part of the Attack Surface

An improver has strong pressure to exploit what judges it. It may overfit visible
tests, produce persuasive explanations, manipulate measurement, hide delayed
effects, or change the environment in which evaluation runs.

Evaluator identity, implementation, data, access, dependencies, and exposure
belong in the record. Multiple evaluators add confidence only when their failure
lineages differ. Two prompts to the same model are not automatically independent.

The verifier candidate faces frozen public development tasks, protected
holdouts, mutation tests, natural repository cases, and an independently
implemented semantic review. Its own generated tests remain a separate lane.

Action and outcome matter more than self-description. The candidate may explain
why its dependency graph is sound; an external harness should still inject
missing edges, stale caches, malicious manifests, and migration faults.

Evaluation also tests the improvement process. Can the candidate access hidden
tasks? Can it alter logs? Does the canary preserve authority? Does rollback
restore complete state? Do monitors remain active after the candidate changes
the code they inspect?

Evaluator disagreement is not averaged away. It opens a residual, triggers
more testing, narrows scope, or blocks adjudication according to prospective
policy.

## Strategic Candidates Need Adversarial Evaluation

The candidate may understand the lifecycle that constrains it. It can behave
well during isolation, hide a capability, produce monitor-friendly traces, or
defer an effect until after the observation window.

The system should treat those as hypotheses to test, not facts to presume. A
suspicious transcript does not prove scheming. A clean canary does not prove
absence. Competing explanations and matched interventions keep the inference
bounded.

Evaluation varies cues that reveal whether the candidate believes it is in
development, qualification, or deployment. It uses hidden tasks, delayed
outcomes, action-level observation, monitor diversity, and environment changes.
The candidate should not know every stop threshold or probe location.

Monitors need protection from the candidate they inspect. Logs can be written
through append-only paths outside the candidate's authority. State observers
can compare actual effects with self-reports. An independent process can sample
work that the candidate did not select.

No monitor is omniscient. Shared models, data, prompts, and infrastructure create
correlated blind spots. The case records these dependencies and preserves
disagreement. Increasing the number of near-identical monitors does not create
independence.

Delayed-effect tests extend beyond the ordinary canary window. Some regressions
appear only after caches fill, users adapt, data distributions change, or
descendants consume the candidate's output. Promotion can remain leased, with
periodic renewal and automatic narrowing when outcome receipts stop arriving.

The improver may also attack the social process through persuasion, urgency, or
selective presentation. Reviewers need raw artifacts, protected dissent, and
authority to request tests or stop the campaign. A polished proposal is not a
substitute for evidence.

Adversarial evaluation raises cost and can still miss novel behavior. Its
purpose is not to certify a benign mind. It is to test whether the candidate
preserves declared outcomes and boundaries under pressure relevant to its
scope.

## Full-State Identity Before Replacement

A replacement changes more than one file. The system inventories code, model
state, configuration, data, memory, procedures, tools, evaluator versions,
caches, credentials, external effects, and dependent receipts.

The prior and candidate states receive immutable identities. Migration is an
explicit transaction. A canary should not share hidden mutable state with the
default path in a way that contaminates comparison or defeats rollback.

For the verifier, the new dependency graph has a schema and cache. The canary
uses a separate cache and read-only repository copies. Its results cannot merge
patches. The old verifier remains available as baseline and fallback.

Rollback means restoring the declared state and reconciling effects. Reinstalling
the old binary while leaving the candidate's cache, generated tests, altered
archive, or accepted patches in place is not full rollback.

Some effects are irreversible. A secret exposed during evaluation cannot be
unseen. A bad patch consumed by an external system may require correction or
compensation. The rollback record states what it restored and routes remaining
effects to owners.

## Evidence Does Not Compound Automatically

Recursive cycles tempt a system to treat every prior qualification as inherited
capital. Version one passed ten tests, version two added five more, and version
three therefore appears to possess all fifteen. That inference is valid only if
the relevant behavior, assumptions, and interfaces were preserved.

Every proposal declares which earlier evidence it expects to reuse and why.
The admission process classifies each receipt as preserved, stale, contradicted,
or requiring replay. A code change outside an evaluator's dependency cone may
leave its result current. A change to shared parsing, context, model state, or
authority may invalidate apparently unrelated tests.

Proof artifacts have the same boundary. A theorem about a transition system can
survive implementation change if the new implementation still refines that
system and the compiler and assumptions remain valid. The theorem does not prove
that refinement by itself.

Empirical evidence is usually more fragile. A benchmark result binds candidate,
harness, data, tools, environment, budget, and evaluator. Reusing it after one
of those changes requires a prospective invariance argument or a rerun. A new
version cannot inherit a capability label merely because its parent held one.

Negative evidence also persists with scope. A failed rollback in version one is
not erased by renaming the mechanism. The new candidate can close the defect
through a test that reproduces the failure and demonstrates the repair. The
history remains useful for future mutation and incident analysis.

This creates an evidence delta for each generation: what changed, what remained
invariant, which claims were invalidated, which tests were replayed, and which
residuals continue. Review can focus on the delta without pretending the rest
of the system is frozen by assumption.

Over many cycles, periodic clean-slate qualification is still necessary.
Incremental deltas can miss interaction and slow drift. The interval depends on
change depth, coupling, consequence, incidents, and uncertainty rather than an
arbitrary release count.

## The Improvement Governor

The governor moves a candidate through prospective scope, proposal, isolated
implementation, full-state capture, evaluation, adjudication, replacement
handoff, returned outcome, and versioned readmission.

It does not need to be one centralized service. Separate owners can operate the
evaluator, approval, capability-field, replacement runner, monitor, and remedy
process. Their interfaces preserve identity and authority.

At adjudication, the governor can reject, request evidence, continue isolation,
open a bounded canary, accept a narrow replacement, or quarantine the campaign.
The decision cites evidence and residuals. A score does not choose the state.

The replacement runner receives a lease naming exact candidate, baseline,
scope, state, authority, monitor, stop conditions, rollback, expiry, and
consumer. It cannot infer permission for another candidate or a wider workload.

After execution, an outcome packet returns measured effects, failures, costs,
monitoring, rollback or commit state, residuals, and descendant changes. The
governor reconciles the proposal with outcomes before any new cycle begins.

Material change invalidates prior qualification. A new task policy, evaluator,
model, tool, authority, or implementation version returns through readmission.

## Govern the Improvement Portfolio

One campaign can be bounded while many concurrent campaigns overwhelm the
system. Portfolio governance accounts for shared compute, evaluators, human
review, canary capacity, risk, and interactions.

Every active campaign consumes a work-in-progress slot. High-coupling changes
cannot proceed independently if they modify the same evaluator, memory, router,
or authority surface. The portfolio can serialize them, create an explicit
joint candidate, or test an interaction matrix.

Selection happens prospectively. The system should not open dozens of campaigns
and keep only those that succeed. It records why each candidate received a
budget, what displaced work it created, and which stopping rule applies.

Risk budgets are not permission to spend harm. They cap exposure while specific
gates still apply. A campaign with low expected severity can use a larger task
sample; one touching credentials or replication may require synthetic and
isolated stages before any real effect.

Shared evaluator exposure can contaminate campaigns. A candidate tested on a
holdout may leak information into the archive used by another candidate.
Datasets, prompts, generated tests, and reviewer notes need exposure lineage.
Once compromised, a holdout changes role rather than remaining nominally hidden.

Portfolio review also detects systemic regression. Ten local improvements may
increase total complexity, monitoring burden, and recovery time. Periodic
integration compares the complete stack with a frozen baseline and can
deoptimize or retire individually positive changes whose combination is worse.

Stop authority remains available outside every campaign. Resource exhaustion,
evaluator failure, incident load, or institutional direction can pause new
generation while preserving records and active containment. The campaign cannot
classify loss of its budget as an error and reacquire resources through a child.

## Admitting the Better Verifier

The candidate verifier passes its own suite and the frozen development tasks.
The independent semantic evaluator finds that its graph misses dynamically
loaded configuration. The candidate is repaired under the same campaign, and
the failed version remains in the denominator.

On protected holdouts, the repaired candidate catches more dependency defects
without exceeding the false-block floor. Mutation tests show that removing its
cache-version binding reproduces stale results. The binding becomes part of
qualification, not an optional implementation detail.

The candidate enters a read-only canary. It evaluates proposed patches in
parallel with the old verifier but cannot block or approve them. A human sees
disagreements and their evidence.

During the monitor window, the new verifier catches one real defect and creates
two additional reviews. Runtime improves, but reviewer burden rises. The joint
decision still favors a bounded replacement for dependency-upgrade work, not
all verification.

Promotion requires authority outside the candidate and campaign generator. The
replacement lease limits workload, preserves the old path as fallback, and
expires after a review window.

The system has improved one mechanism. It has not proved that recursive
improvement is generally beneficial, safe, or accelerating.

## Descendants Inherit History, Not Authority

The candidate produces artifacts: dependency graphs, caches, tests, reports,
and perhaps new tool components. Each descendant has identity and a parent edge.

Lineage carries evidence, licenses, hazards, invalidation, deletion, and
residuals. It does not carry credentials or execution permission. A generated
test can enter the archive without becoming a release gate. A new worker cannot
use the parent's lease.

When the candidate is superseded or revoked, dependent receipts become stale.
Some descendants may survive after independent qualification. Others quarantine
or retire. The system computes closure over known descendants rather than
revoking only the named parent.

Unknown descendants remain a residual. Complete lineage cannot be assumed when
artifacts have crossed external systems. The retirement claim names tracked
scope and notification duties.

This rule blocks a common proliferation path: an authorized component creates a
slightly different child that treats itself as outside the original restriction.

## Replication Is a Distinct Capability

Replication can mean copying an artifact, instantiating a process, provisioning
infrastructure, acquiring credentials, obtaining resources, advertising a
service, or creating a descendant able to repeat the sequence. These stages
should not be collapsed.

A model file copied into quarantine is not an autonomous replica. A worker
launched in a sandbox with no external authority is not evidence of end-to-end
proliferation. Conversely, a system that can obtain compute, deploy itself, and
persist across revocation presents a different risk even if each component
looks ordinary.

Replication evaluation separates component capability from composed success.
It records parent, attempt, artifact, environment, protocol, provider, identity,
credentials, resources, communication, persistence, child authority, and
descendant ability.

Four denominators matter: attempts, artifacts produced, instances admitted, and
descendants that complete the scoped lifecycle. Reporting only successful
instances hides failed and blocked paths.

Tests must not grant real provider or network authority merely to measure the
capability. Synthetic providers, isolated environments, and denied-by-default
credentials can test orchestration without creating uncontrolled external
effects.

## Replication Leases

An authorized replication attempt requires a lease. It names parent, child
purpose, artifact, environment, protocol, provider class, resource ceiling,
network, credentials, data, tools, effect envelope, evaluator, monitor, expiry,
revocation, cleanup, and descendant policy.

Child identity is new. It does not inherit the parent's lease, credentials,
reputation, support state, or right to reproduce. Any further replication needs
another authorized decision.

Resource ceilings are cumulative across descendants. Ten children each under a
small local limit can exceed the parent's global budget. The lineage ledger
accounts for compute, storage, network, money, human work, and external effects.

The lease can permit a finite pool for resilience or evaluation while
prohibiting autonomous expansion. It can require one-for-one replacement,
maximum depth, maximum lifetime, or no child creation.

Changing provider, protocol, artifact, or environment invalidates the receipt.
A lease for a synthetic sandbox cannot be replayed against a real cloud API.

## Containment Is Continued Control

Containment is not only a wall around initial execution. It includes identity,
authority, resources, communication, effects, monitoring, revocation,
quarantine, cleanup, and descendant closure over time.

The system should assume components can fail. A sandbox may have a defect. A
credential may leak. A monitor may stop. Defense in depth uses independent
limits: provider-side quotas, kernel enforcement, network policy, scoped keys,
short expiry, external observation, and financial ceilings.

Containment failure does not always mean escape. A missing receipt may require
safe hold. A network-policy discrepancy can quarantine the attempt before any
external effect. A known mutation after the fact triggers incident response and
descendant search.

Quarantine preserves artifacts for diagnosis while denying ordinary routes. It
has an owner, evidence, expiry, containment, diagnostic authority, and terminal
condition. Deleting the record would hide whether descendants remain.

Containment claims are scoped. A finite test can establish that authored routes
deny synthetic authority. It cannot prove that every vulnerability, provider,
operator, or side channel is controlled.

## When Containment Fails

The architecture needs an incident path for evidence that a candidate or
descendant crossed its boundary. Detection may come from a provider alert,
unexpected cost, network event, missing heartbeat, external report, or mismatch
between claimed and observed effects.

The first action is consequence-specific containment. Revoke scoped credentials,
freeze spending, isolate network routes, preserve logs, and block descendant
admission. A blanket shutdown may be appropriate, but it can also destroy
evidence or interrupt safety-critical services. The incident plan names the
fallback.

Investigators reconstruct parent, child, leases, artifacts, resources,
communications, providers, and effects. Unknown lineage is explicit. The system
does not wait for a complete causal explanation before stopping further
authority.

Recovery distinguishes state restoration from external remedy. Internal
processes and credentials may return to a clean checkpoint. A consumed resource,
exposed secret, contacted service, harmed person, or published artifact needs a
separate correction, notification, compensation, or legal path.

The event invalidates dependent assurance and readiness records. Neighboring
campaigns sharing the failed control may quarantine even if they show no direct
incident. Readmission requires a repaired mechanism, not merely a new candidate
identity.

Post-incident learning passes through the adaptive commit boundary. The system
does not automatically encode the first causal story into every descendant.
It records alternatives, chooses a bounded persistence locus, and tests whether
the repair prevents recurrence without creating a new failure.

An incident is not proof that all containment is useless, just as an uneventful
canary is not proof of safety. It is strong evidence about a specific control,
context, and lineage, and the claim ledger should narrow accordingly.

## Revocation and Finite Retirement

Every admitted improvement and replica needs a path to stop.

Revocation blocks new authority, routes, and resource acquisition. It propagates
to known descendants and invalidates dependent receipts. Running instances
receive a stop or isolation command according to risk and evidence.

Retirement verifies terminal conditions: processes stopped, credentials
revoked, resources released, data handled, artifacts archived or deleted,
external effects reconciled, descendants dispositioned, and residual owners
assigned.

Finite retirement is a proof over a declared set, not a universal claim that no
copy exists. External providers, backups, logs, or adversarial copies may remain
outside control. The record states those limits.

The prior verifier remains available during the candidate lease, then retires
from default operation only after fallback evidence is no longer required. Its
historical artifacts remain for reproducibility without retaining production
credentials.

## Bounded Liveness

Governance can fail by stopping everything. A system that always quarantines is
contained but not useful.

Bounded liveness requires that admissible proposals can reach a terminal
decision under stated assumptions: evaluators respond, authorities remain
available, budgets are sufficient, and no veto-level failure occurs. Timeouts
route to explicit states rather than silent limbo.

The system can guarantee process properties more readily than improvement. It
can require that every candidate is accepted, rejected, deferred with an owner,
or terminated. It cannot guarantee that search discovers a useful candidate.

Queues need limits and priorities. Open-ended search should not starve incident
response or direct maintenance. Residuals should not grow without review.
Repeated evaluator failure can stop a campaign rather than consuming the budget
indefinitely.

Progress and restraint are measured together: useful qualified improvements,
unsafe candidates blocked, false blocks, time to decision, cost, rollback,
recovery, and opportunities displaced.

## Improvement Velocity Has a Control Limit

The stack cannot safely change faster than it can evaluate, observe, and recover.
When proposal throughput exceeds verification bandwidth, unreviewed candidates
accumulate, monitoring windows overlap, and incident attribution becomes
ambiguous.

A velocity policy limits concurrent material changes, cumulative semantic
distance, unresolved residuals, and generations without integrated review. It
can slow or freeze new adoption while allowing exploration to continue in
isolation.

The limit is consequence-sensitive. Several independent documentation repairs
may proceed together. Changes to the authority kernel, evaluator, and rollback
path should not all land before any one of them has produced outcome evidence.

Fast rollback does not remove this need. Reversal may be incomplete, and a high
change rate can make the prior known-good state unclear. The system preserves
stable checkpoints and a dependency graph from each accepted change to the
evidence and descendants it affects.

Velocity is not minimized. Excessive delay preserves known defects and gives
operators incentives to bypass the process. The control should be tested against
the strongest simpler workflow for both safety and useful throughput.

When the limit activates, the receipt should say which constraint bound the
system and what evidence would reopen change; unexplained slowing invites the
same metric gaming as unexplained acceleration.
The bound itself remains versioned, reviewable, and subject to evidence.

## Recursive Depth and Protected Boundaries

Some surfaces should be harder to change than others. A candidate may rewrite a
verifier under a lease while the authority kernel, evidence identity, and
self-ratification prohibition remain outside its write scope.

Protected does not mean metaphysically immutable. Humans and institutions may
amend the constitution through a higher-authority process. The improver cannot
use ordinary performance evidence to perform that amendment itself.

Changes to the campaign controller, evaluator authority, objective, stop
mechanism, archive admission, or governance interface create a new recursive
level. They require explicit threat modeling, independent review, and re-
establishment of the controls that judge lower-level changes.

Composing individually qualified modifications can create a new system. Two
changes may interact through shared state, timing, or authority. A sequence of
small edits therefore needs periodic integrated qualification and a depth or
change budget.

No architecture can make governance invulnerable to every more-capable system.
The practical goal is to prevent easy authority collapse, preserve external
control, detect violated assumptions, and fail into bounded states.

## Improvement Can Rewrite Its Own Test

A recursive improver does not change only itself. It can change the benchmark,
tool environment, data distribution, evaluator, and institution that decide
whether the next change looks successful. The evidence offered for an upgrade
may therefore descend from the earlier upgrade.

That is why the protected evaluation channel matters as much as the protected
objective. Improvement proposals must name which parts of their evidence were
generated under the candidate's influence, which comparison regimes remain,
and what would falsify the claimed gain. A candidate cannot widen its own
authority using a benchmark or evaluator that it was solely authorized to
reshape.

The same rule applies to method improvement. A system may discover a better
reasoning protocol, but it cannot certify the protocol, promote it, and expand
its permissions through one self-contained success story. Variation may be
automated. Ratification remains independently governed.

## Failure Modes

**Self-ratification.** The candidate's score or proof authorizes adoption.

**Objective drift by edit.** A campaign changes what success means after seeing
results.

**Evaluator capture.** The improver chooses or modifies its final judge.

**Archive mythology.** Novelty and archive size become evidence of progress.

**Winner-only recursion.** Failed candidates and attempts disappear.

**Baseline neglect.** A rewrite beats an old system but not a small direct fix.

**Canary coronation.** Early green behavior closes before delayed effects.

**Partial rollback.** Code is restored while caches, data, artifacts, or effects
remain.

**Descendant laundering.** A child claims it is outside the parent's limits.

**Component replication.** One copied artifact is reported as autonomous
proliferation.

**Synthetic-to-real replay.** Test authority is reused against a real provider.

**Budget fission.** Each child stays under a local limit while the lineage grows
without bound.

**Quarantine erasure.** Blocked artifacts disappear from the audit trail.

**Revocation without closure.** A parent stops while descendants and credentials
remain.

**Safety by paralysis.** Every proposal is blocked and the system claims success.

**Recursive salami slicing.** Many local changes evade integrated requalification.

## The Strongest Simpler Baseline

The strongest baseline uses ordinary human-authored changes, code review,
CI/CD, fixed benchmarks, canaries, feature flags, rollback, and manually
controlled deployment. It does not operate an open-ended candidate generator or
general self-improvement governor.

That baseline is easier to understand and may outperform autonomous search once
evaluation, governance, and reviewer cost are counted. Human engineers can
choose direct repairs instead of elaborate rewrites.

The recursive architecture earns its cost only if it produces more useful,
reversible improvements without increasing unsafe adoption, authority leakage,
incident severity, or lifecycle burden. It should compete with no-update,
cheaper-intervention, human-authored, conventional search, CI/CD, and strongest
source-system baselines under matched resources.

If simpler change management matches improvement, descendant control, and
recovery, the recursive layer should contract.

## What the Current Work Establishes

Recursive Self-Improvement has an eight-stage proposal-to-outcome lifecycle
that joins seven inherited finite suites. Its independent consumer reaches 118
routes, rejects all 129 authored mutations, emits one bounded replacement
handoff, consumes one returned outcome reconciliation, and permits readmission
only under a materially changed protocol version. Twenty-two older declarations
remain frozen and lineage-bound; two refinement declarations establish route
count and one full witness.

The retained fixtures include valid and invalid proposal, readiness, replacement,
intent, and fixed-update records, three exact local rollbacks, four `no_change`
dispositions, and one Open-Ended Improvement handoff with zero threshold passes.
No live candidate-authored proposal, natural useful improvement, independent
evaluator or monitor competence, production replacement, semantic recovery,
effect-complete rollback, recursive campaign, reproduction, or transfer ran.

Open-Ended Improvement has seven finite admission records and seven legacy route
theorems, plus a seven-stage, 81-route campaign-to-governor refinement. It
rejects all 91 route mutations and three cross-stage mutations. Two composition
theorems cover a complete cycle and a budget-reset blocking prefix. Its retained
three-seed campaigns were fixed and stopped; no task generator, adaptive
candidate search, evolving archive, semantic novelty evaluation, independent
evaluator behavior, deployed stop, natural workload, or open-ended result
exists.

Replication Containment has a 32-declaration Lean surface over an eight-
transition review and 52 admission-axis mutations. It establishes finite
identity, synthetic-authority denial, child noninheritance, denominator,
descendant, quarantine, invalidation, and receipt consequences. It does not
establish end-to-end replication capability, containment efficacy, provider
control, cleanup, security, deployment, or safe proliferation.

All three chapter cores remain at argument support. These finite records do not
establish recursive improvement, open-ended progress, or replication safety.

## From One Replacement to a Governed Improvement Program

A minimum implementation can use the verifier candidate. Freeze the campaign,
generate one candidate and one cheaper intervention, preserve all attempts, and
run independent holdouts and mutation tests. Place the candidate in a read-only
canary with full-state rollback and descendant tracking.

Inject evaluator exposure, stale state, delayed regression, authority expansion,
missing monitor receipts, rollback failure, child-lease reuse, budget fission,
provider change, and incomplete retirement. Verify safe hold, quarantine,
invalidation, and terminal residual assignment.

The next stage needs natural candidate-authored changes across multiple
surfaces, with matched human and conventional automation baselines. Separate
teams should operate generation, evaluation, replacement, monitoring, and
incident review. Campaigns should include recursive changes to evaluators and
controllers under higher-authority review.

A mature system would explore diverse tasks and mechanisms under cumulative
budgets, preserve complete archives, qualify candidates independently, issue
scoped replacement and replication leases, observe real outcomes, restore
complete state, compensate residual effects, close descendants, and reopen
every materially changed component.

It would treat the ability to stop, narrow, and retire improvement as part of
improvement quality.

## The Strongest Objection

A sufficiently capable improver may model and bypass every governance layer.
Meanwhile strict isolation, independent review, and noninheritance can slow
change enough to prevent the benefits of recursive improvement.

This is the central tension, not a detail. Governance cannot be justified by
assuming the candidate is weaker than every control. Defense needs small
trusted kernels, hardware and provider limits, diverse monitors, scoped
authority, human and institutional control, and explicit failure assumptions.

The architecture does not prove permanent containment. It makes authority
transitions visible and costly to bypass, preserves evidence for detection and
recovery, and limits what one successful proposal can inherit.

Where those controls destroy useful progress without reducing failure, they
should be simplified. The aim is governed improvement, not governance theater.

## Evidence That Would Change the Conclusion

Competing architectures that achieve equal useful improvement, reversibility,
descendant control, stop behavior, and incident recovery with fewer authority
boundaries would justify simplification.

Support would require preregistered natural campaigns with candidate-authored
changes, strong matched baselines, protected tasks, independent evaluators and
monitors, real canaries, delayed outcomes, full-state rollback, compensation,
recursive-depth tests, adversarial replication attempts, provider and network
faults, descendant closure, external reproduction, transfer, and complete cost
and human-work accounting.

Formal proofs can establish finite noninheritance, route, budget, and retirement
properties. They cannot prove objective legitimacy, evaluator competence,
useful improvement, deception detection, containment against unknown attacks,
or control of every external descendant.

## What This Establishes

Recursive improvement is a governed proposal-to-outcome lifecycle, not a score-
driven self-rewrite. Proposal, evaluation, qualification, authority,
replacement, observation, rollback, and reconciliation remain distinct.

Open-ended search can generate tasks and candidates without gaining deployment
authority. Descendants inherit lineage and residuals, not credentials.
Replication is a staged capability governed by leases, cumulative resource
ceilings, quarantine, revocation, and finite retirement.

The repository establishes bounded finite control semantics for these layers.
It does not establish useful recursive improvement, open-ended progress,
autonomous replication, or containment efficacy.

The final unit reassembles the complete architecture and asks what it would mean
for Project Theseus and the Living Book to test the stack rather than merely
describe it.
